'''Raphael Max Littauer''' (November 28, 1925 – October 19, 2009) was an American physicist who was a longtime Professor of Physics and Nuclear Studies at [[Cornell University]].  He was involved in the development of several [[particle accelerator]]s there, in particular the 10 GeV electron synchrotron at the [[Wilson Synchrotron Lab]] in the late 1960s, where he devised a distributed, multiplexed control system for it, and the  [[Cornell Electron Storage Ring]] (CESR) in the late 1970s and early 1980s, where his scheme to create pretzel-shaped orbits to increase the number of particle bunches in circulation contributed significantly to CESR having the highest [[Luminosity (scattering theory)|luminosity]] of any accelerator of its era.  Littauer was also known for his teaching, including the design, implementation, and installation of one of the earliest and most successful [[classroom response system]]s.  An [[opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War|active opponent of the Vietnam War]], he led a group at Cornell that published a well-regarded study on the nature and effects of the U.S. air attacks in Southeast Asia. In 1991 he became a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and in 1995 he received the [[Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators]].

== Early life and education ==
Littauer was born in [[Leipzig]], Germany, on November 28, 1925.<ref name="DeG-bio"/>  In March 1939 he emigrated to the United Kingdom,<ref name="DeG-bio"/> six months before the outbreak of [[World War II]].<ref name="cornell-obit"/>  According to what his daughter later related, he was part of the ''[[Kindertransport]]'' and was taken in by a family in England.<ref name="celia-about">{{cite web | url=https://celia-clement.com/about/ | title=About: Celia Clement | publisher=Celia-clement.com | access-date=February 10, 2023}}</ref>

He attended the [[University of Cambridge]] beginning in 1943.<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/> He first received an [[M.A.]] degree,<ref name="camb-abs"/> that being awarded in 1946.<ref name="DeG-bio"/> He then earned a [[Ph.D.]] from [[Christ's College, Cambridge|Christ's College]] at Cambridge in 1950,<ref name="aps-award-1995"/> the title of his dissertation being ''Levels in Light Elements''.<ref name="camb-abs">{{cite book | title=Abstracts of Dissertations Approved for the Ph. D., M. Sc., and M. Litt. Degrees in the University of Cambridge During the Academical Year | publisher=Cambridge University Press | year=1949 | page=210 }}</ref> During this time he worked as an assistant in the famed [[Cavendish Laboratory]].<ref name="DeG-bio"/>

== Marriage and family ==
Littauer married Salome Alexandra Kroch in 1950.<ref name="DeG-bio"/>  Also born in Leipzig,<ref name="celia-about"/> she and her two sisters had endured a hazardous journey through Europe in order to survive the Holocaust.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://iaujc.org/holocaust-education/oral-histories-and-books-local-interest | title=Oral Histories and Books of Local Interest | publisher=Ithaca Area United Jewish Community | access-date=February 6, 2024}} See also {{cite web | url=https://ithacavoice.org/2022/04/eighth-annual-holocaust-memorial-day-lecture-april-27/ | title=Eighth annual Holocaust Memorial Day lecture April 27  | publisher=The Ithaca Voice | date=April 7, 2022}}</ref>

Littauer left England for the United States in 1950,<ref name="DeG-bio"/> becoming a research associate at [[Cornell University]].<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>  Together  he and his wife had two children.<ref name="DeG-bio"/> The couple lived in [[Ithaca, New York]].<ref name="ij-1962"/> Alexandra Littauer taught French in the younger grades of the [[Ithaca City School District]]<ref name="alexandra-obit"/> and later became an instructor in French at Cornell.<ref name="ann-cas-74-75"/>

Raphael Littauer became a [[United States citizen]] in 1956.<ref name="DeG-bio">{{cite book | url=https://www.degruyter.com/database/BHDE/entry/BHB-6719/html <!-- https://www-degruyter-com.wikipedialibrary.idm.oclc.org/database/BHDE/entry/BHB-6719/html -->| chapter=Littauer, Raphael Max | title=Biographisches Handbuch der deutschsprachigen Emigration nach 1933 | volume=2 (The Arts, Sciences, and Literature) | editor-first=Werner | editor-last=Röder | editor2-first= Herbert A. | editor2-last=Strauss| publisher=K. G. Saur | year=1983 | location=München | page=738 | isbn=3-598-10089-2 | language=DE| via= De Gruyter Oldenbourg, 2022 }}</ref>

== Career as physicist ==
=== Accelerators and positions ===
[[Image:Laboratory of Nuclear Studies, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York. LOC gsc.5a21402.jpg|thumb|upright|left|A room within the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies at Cornell, 1952]]
Littauer's arrival at Cornell    in 1950 was in order to do work on  an  [[electron accelerator]] at Cornell's Laboratory for Nuclear Studies,<ref name="cornell-obit">{{cite web | url=https://hdl.handle.net/1813/112502 <!-- https://ecommons.cornell.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/be16f001-d542-478a-9de6-7dc7451c7631/content --> | title=Memorial Statement for Raphael M. Littauer | author-first=Donald | author-last=Holcomb | author2-first=Ahren | author2-last=Sadoff | author3-first=Maury | author3-last=Tigner | publisher=Cornell University Library | date=2009 }}</ref> which had been founded after World War II by scientists returning to academic life following their  [[Project Y|efforts at Los Alamos]].<ref name="cerncourier-2002">{{cite news | url=https://cerncourier.com/a/cornells-laboratory-is-at-the-crossroads/ | title=Cornell's laboratory is at the crossroads | magazine=CERN Courier | date=January 25, 2002}}</ref> The director of that laboratory, [[Robert R. Wilson]], was instrumental in bringing Littauer there.<ref name="rrw-papers">{{cite web | url=https://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/RMA03093.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040326091638/http://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/RMA03093.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 26, 2004 | title=Robert R. Wilson papers, 1936–2000. Collection Number: 14-22-3093 | publisher=Division of Rare and Manuscript Collections, Cornell University Library | access-date=February 14, 2024}}</ref> At the time Cornell had a 300 MeV electron synchrotron, which was followed in 1952 by a new 1.3 GeV synchrotron.<ref name="cornell-accelerators-legacy">{{cite journal | url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-nucl-102014-021850 | title=The Legacy of Cornell Accelerators | first1=M. | last1=Tigner | first2=D.G. | last2=Cassel | journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science | publisher=Annual Reviews | year=2015 | volume=65 | issue=1 | pages= 1–23 | doi=10.1146/annurev-nucl-102014-021850 | bibcode=2015ARNPS..65....1T | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1954, Littauer departed Cornell to work on a synchrotron at the [[General Electric Research Laboratory]] in [[Schenectady, New York]].<ref name="DeG-bio"/><ref name="cornell-obit"/> But in 1955, Littauer returned to Cornell for good, being appointed a member of the faculty as a Research Associate Professor of Physics.<ref name="DeG-bio"/><ref name="cornell-obit"/> Once again, Wilson played a role in his return.<ref name="rrw-papers"/><!-- didn't find anything independent on the “kick-sorter” --><!-- THIS IS GETTING TOO LONG, TOO DETAILED.   SHORTER IS BETTER ... -->

In 1963, Littauer was named a research professor.<ref name="DeG-bio"/>   Then in 1965, he became a full professor,<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>  being named a professor of Physics and Nuclear Studies.<ref name="DeG-bio"/>

Littauer was awarded two postdoctoral fellowships from the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>  The second of these, in 1968, involved work at the [[Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati]] in Italy.<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>  There he spent a semester working on the laboratory's new 1.5 GeV electron-positron [[colliding beam accelerator]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19680129.2.24&srpos=4&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-raphael+littauer------ | title=Three Professors Honored | newspaper=The Cornell Daily Sun | date=January 29, 1968 | page=5 }}</ref>

<!-- see also for some context https://www.chess.cornell.edu/about/history -->Later in 1968, Cornell's Wilson Synchrotron Laboratory saw the dedication of its new 10 GeV [[electron synchrotron]], the largest and most powerful such one in the world, with Littauer highlighted as one of the people who helped develop it.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19681010.2.32&srpos=5&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-raphael+littauer------ | title=Cornell Machine World's Largest | first1=Matthew | last1=Feinstein | first2=Sam | last2=Pizzigati | newspaper=The Cornell Daily Sun | date=October 10, 1968 | page=1 }}</ref>  The ring  was built underneath [[Schoellkopf Field]] and other athletic facilities on campus.<ref name="cerncourier-2002"/> Among Littauer's responsibilities were monitoring and adjusting the steering coils located around the synchrotron's ring .<ref>{{cite news | url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19681010.2.35&srpos=6&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-raphael+littauer------ | title=Synchrotron Story: How It Shoots Electrons | newspaper=The Cornell Daily Sun | date=October 10, 1968 | pages=8–9 }}</ref> As part of his work, Littauer created a time-sharing, distributed, multiplex control system for the synchrotron that helped reduce both the initial and ongoing costs of the system.<ref name="cornell-accelerators-legacy"/><ref name="cornell-obit"/>

[[Image:Cornell Wilson Wilson Synchrotron Lab (Spring 2023) 3.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|right|A portion of the Cornell Electron Storage Ring (CESR) tunnel, as seen in 2023]]
The [[Cornell Electron Storage Ring]] (CESR) came into operation at the end of 1970s but initially featured disappointing  [[Luminosity (scattering theory)|luminosity]], so over the next several years several improvements to it were made.<ref name="cornell-accelerators-legacy"/> One of them, put into place in 1983,<ref name="cerncourier-1995"/> was Littauer's development of a scheme for so-called "pretzel orbits" (a name he came up with).<ref name="talman">{{cite conference | contribution=THT4B2 – Single Ring Multibunch Operation and Beam Separation | first=Richard | last=Talman | title=HF2014: Proceedings of the 55th ICFA Advanced Beam Dynamics Workshop on High Luminosity Circular e+e- Colliders – Higgs Factory | location= Beijing, China | date=2014 | pages=33&ndash;39 }}</ref> This involved having multiple bunches of particles in a [[storage ring]], but introducing [[electrostatic separator]]s at key places in the ring such that two counter-circulating beams are displaced in eccentric and opposite directions, thereby limiting the number of collisions in a rotation and increasing the number of bunches that can be in circulation.<ref name="cerncourier-1995"/><ref name="talman"/><ref name="OHAIP-Tigner"/> With this among other improvements, throughout the 1990s, CESR had the highest luminosity of any colliding-beam system in the world and became valuable as a [[synchrotron light source]]<ref name="cornell-accelerators-legacy"/> The pretzel orbits scheme was subsequently embraced and successfully incorporated into the [[Tevatron]] particle accelerator at [[Fermilab]] and the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider]] at [[CERN]].<ref name="cerncourier-1995">{{cite news | url=http://cds.cern.ch/record/1732434/files/vol35-issue6-p011-e.pdf | title=Cornell: Bunch trains provide higher luminosity| magazine=CERN Courier | date=September 1995 | pages=11&ndash;12, 14}} Also "American Physical Society beams recognition", p. 14.</ref>

Overall, the physicist [[Maury Tigner]] has described Littauer as someone who was "very much interested in accelerators and was ... a pioneering controls designer and builder."<ref name="OHAIP-Tigner">{{cite interview |last=Tigner |first=Maury |subject-link= |interviewer=
David Zierler |title=Interview of Maury Tigner by David Zierler|work= |date=    February 15, 2021|publisher=Niels Bohr Library & Archives, American Institute of Physics |location= College Park, Maryland |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/47091 }}</ref>

<!-- doesn't seem of lasting significance, leave out In 1969, Littauer headed a summertime committee that investigated the different interpretations of [[academic freedom]]<ref>{{cite news | url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19690925.2.35&srpos=7&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-raphael+littauer------ | title=Acad. Freedom Position Urged |  first=Richard L. | last=Neubauer | newspaper=The Cornell Daily Sun | date=September 25, 1969 | page=11 }}</ref> -->In 1974, Littauer was elected chair of Cornell's department of physics,<ref name="sps-chair-bio">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-post-standard/140713250/ | title=Elect Littauer Chairman | newspaper=The Post-Standard | location=Syracuse, New York | date=July 25, 1974 | page=26 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> a department which held 47 faculty members at the time.<ref name="ann-cas-74-75">{{cite book | title=Cornell University Announcements: College of Arts and Sciences: 1974&ndash;75 | publisher=Cornell University | year=1974 | pages=132, 162 }}</ref>  He remained in that position for three years.<ref name="DeG-bio"/>

=== Research ===
{{expand section|date=September 2024}}
In addition to his work on accelerator construction and operation, Littauer was the author or co-author of a number of articles in physics journals.<ref>See for instance [https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C31&q=raphael+littauer&oq= this search].</ref>  In 1958, he was one of several groups that published results regarding [[Nucleon#Nucleon resonances|nucleon resonances]], finding and establishing the properties of the state latter known as [[Nucleon#Nucleon resonances|N(1520)]].<ref name="cornell-accelerators-legacy"/>

=== Teaching ===
[[Image:Cornell Rockefeller Hall.jpg|thumb|left|Rockefeller Hall on the Cornell campus, where Littauer's electronic classroom response system was installed]]
<!-- nothing of use in the Announcements -->Littauer had a longtime interest in how the teaching of physics, and teaching in general, could be improved.<ref name="ij-obit-2009"/><ref name="cornell-obit"/>  This included giving out lecture notes that emphasized scientific understanding coming out of mathematical formulae and experiments that could be performed in class.<ref name="ij-obit-2009"/><ref name="cornell-obit"/>

[[Image:Cornell syllabus and teaching materials for Physics 214.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|right|Physics 214: Optics, Waves, and Particles, Fall 1973: Littauer's syllabus, notes on the classroom response system, and a handout with an instance of the response system questions and answer choices]]
Having seen that large [[lecture hall]] courses such as those given at Cornell tended to result in disengaged or absent students,<ref name="et-impl"/> during 1971 Littauer designed, built, and introduced an electronic [[classroom response system]] into his teaching of physics.<ref name="cc-clicking">{{cite news | url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2006/02/clicking-class-helps-lecturers-and-students-connect | title=Clicking in class helps lecturers from appearing remote by using student remotes as instructional tool  | first= Leslie | last=Intemann | work=Cornell Chronicle | date=February 20, 2006 }}</ref> It allowed the instructor to pose multiple-choice questions to the students, from which they would push buttons at their seats to anonymously register what they thought the answer was, giving the instructor immediate feedback as to students' level of understanding of the material being presented.<ref name="cc-clicking"/> The system was meant for large lecture classes and was permanently installed,<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/> with the location being the Rockefeller B room in the campus's Rockefeller Hall.<ref name="cc-clicking"/>  As such, it was the first such response system at Cornell,<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/> and one of the first such anywhere in the country.<ref name="abrahamson"/> In Fall 1972, Littauer published an account of the system, including photographs of the apparatus as it appeared both to students in their seats and to the teacher at the lectern, in the journal ''Educational Technology''.<ref name="et-impl">{{cite journal | last=Littauer | first=Raphael | title=Instructional Implications of a Low-Cost Electronic Student Response System | journal=Educational Technology | volume=12 | number= 10 | date=October 1972 | pages= 69&ndash;71 | jstor=44419363 | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/44419363 }}</ref> He continued to use it in all his classes.<ref name="cc-clicking"/>

More so than with most such early efforts, Littauer's system was successful, with one later analysis attributing that success to the fact that the designer of the system was also the teacher who used it.<ref name="abrahamson">{{cite book | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=As2tPOKVh8MC&dq=raphael+littauer&pg=PA80 | title=Online and Distance Learning: Concepts, Methodologies, Tools, and Applications: Concepts, Methodologies, Tools, and Applications | editor-last=Tomei | editor-first= Lawrence A. | publisher=IGI Global | year= 2007 | chapter=A Brief History of Networked Classrooms | first=Louis | last=Abrahamson | pages=78&ndash;100| isbn=978-1-59904-936-6 }} At pp.  79&ndash;80, 85.</ref> Although other [[audience response]] technologies emerged over time and were utilized at Cornell, Littauer's system was still in place and in use within Rockefeller B some three decades later.<ref name="cc-clicking"/>

== Anti-war activities ==
In 1962, Littauer was one of two dozen Cornell professors that signed onto a Committee for Peaceful Alternatives, an entity that was looking to run a candidate for [[New York's 33rd congressional district]] in the [[1962 United States House of Representatives elections]] who would have better ideas for finding a solution to the [[nuclear arms race]].<ref name="ij-1962">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-ithaca-journal-jwd-1962-signed-lette/42934348/ | title='Peaceful Alternatives' Group Seeks Candidate | first=Donald | last=Greet | newspaper=The Ithaca Journal | date=February 28, 1962 | page=7 | via=Newspapers.com}} <!-- also https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19620313.2.5&srpos=1&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-raphael+littauer------ --></ref>  
Littauer also became a national council member of the [[Federation of American Scientists]].<ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>

With [[opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War]] being a major issue on American campuses, Littauer became one of the more outspoken members of the faculty in this regard.<ref name="reppy">{{cite book | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lAjtEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA73| title=Beyond Borders: Exploring the History of Cornell's Global Dimensions | editor-first=Royal D. | editor-last=Colle | editor2-first=Heike | editor2-last=Michelsen | editor3-first= Elaine D. | editor3-last=Engst | editor4-first=Corey Ryan | editor4-last=Earle | publisher=Cornell University Press | year=2024 | pages= 73&ndash;78| chapter=Launching Peace Studies at Cornell: The Air War in Indochina | author-first=Judith | author-last=Reppy | location=Ithaca, New York | isbn=978-1-5017-7702-8 }}</ref> This including him being one of a number of physics faculty who stated they would not engage in teaching activities during the [[Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam]] in October 1969 and instead encouraged others to join them.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/?a=d&d=CDS19691003.2.33.1&srpos=3&e=-------en-20--1-byDA-txt-txIN-littauer+vietnam------ | title=Advertisement | newspaper=The Cornell Daily Sun | date=October 3, 1969 | page=10}}</ref>

Starting in May 1971, Littauer headed the Air War Study Group, which was sponsored by Cornell's [[Mario Einaudi Center for International Studies|Center for International Studies]] and consisted of a 19-person group of professors and students who investigated the nature of [[List of bombs in the Vietnam War|the air attacks being conducted]] by the [[United States in the Vietnam War]].<ref name="nyt-1971"/>  They used only unclassified sources and discussions;<ref name="nysean">{{cite web | url=https://www.nysean.org/events/2022/4/21/revisiting-the-air-war-in-indochina-american-strategic-bombing-from-vietnam-to-the-present-expmr | title=Revisiting the Air War in Indochina: American Strategic Bombing From Vietnam to the Present | date=21 April 2022 | publisher=New York Southeast Asia Network | access-date=February 24, 2024}}</ref> as part of this Littauer made trips to Washington to interview participants.<ref name="reppy"/>  The report from the five-month study was distributed privately in November 1971; it established that despite the ongoing [[Vietnamization]] of the ground effort, the United States was still maintaining the air war with large numbers of munitions being delivered, akin to 1967 levels, but that these attacks were ineffective at halting Communist operations in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia.<ref name="nyt-1971"/> The report was written in a matter-of-fact way;<ref name="nytbr-1972"/> while it was motivated by opposition to the war,   Littauer said the study group was trying to be scholarly and fair in their work.<ref name="nyt-1971">{{cite news | url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1971/11/08/79164040.html?pageNumber=6 | title=Study Shows U.S. Presses Air War | first=Neil | last=Sheehan | newspaper=The New York Times | date=November 8, 1971 | page=6 }} Also carried by other papers, see for instance {{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/532056574/?terms=littauer%20%22cornell%20study%20says%22&match=1 | title=Cornell Study Says U.S. Escalates Indochina Air War | agency=New York Times News Service | newspaper=The Berkshire Eagle | date=November 10, 1971 | page=28 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

The study was subsequently revised and updated and published as ''The Air War in Indochina'' in August 1972 by the [[Beacon Press]].<ref name="nytns-aug72">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-oklahoman/139077431/ | title=New Selections | agency=New York Times News Service | newspaper=The Sunday Oklahoman | location=Oklahoma City | date=August 27, 1972 | page=8 (Showcase) | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> By now the study group comprised some 21 scholars encompassing a number of different academic fields.<ref name="nytbr-1972"/> Littauer was joined as editor of the volume by [[Norman Uphoff]], a young professor of government at Cornell.<ref name="nytns-aug72"/>  <!--TODO? Also professor of neurobiology [[Frank Rosenblatt]], professor of astronomy [[Carl Sagan]],    p xii -->  A lengthy, front-page assessment of the volume in a positive vein appeared in the ''[[New York Times Book Review]]''.<ref name="nytbr-1972">{{cite news | url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1972/08/13/91340620.pdf?pdf_redirect=true&ip=0 | title=The bonus and the onus: The Air War In Indochina | first=Robert | last=Kleiman | work=New York Times Book Review | date=August 13, 1972 | pages=1, 2, 14, 15}}</ref>

In a September 1972 [[op-ed]] run by the [[Los Angeles Times News Service]], Littauer decried the air war as  "remote, inefficient and indiscriminate", especially in the use of [[aerial gunship]]s, [[cluster bomb]]s, [[napalm]], and [[Operation Arc Light|B-52 Arc Light saturation bombing]]. Littauer did acknowledge the advent of "smart" [[laser-guided bomb]]s as an improvement, but noted that their existence was not lowering the amount of conventional bombing being done.<ref name="latns-1972">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/austin-american-statesman/138569601/ | title=Use of Bombs in Vietnam War Questioned as Correct 'Tools' | first=Raphael | last=Littauer | agency=Los Angeles Times News Service | newspaper=Austin American-Statesman | date=September 9, 1972 | page=5 | via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Decades later, the study was still being used as a source for analyses of the U.S. air effort.<ref>See for instance {{cite book | url=https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/Portals/10/AUPress/Books/B_0040_TILFORD_SETUP.pdf | last=Tilford | first=Earl H. | title=Setup: What the Air Force Did in Vietnam and Why | location=Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama | publisher= Air University Press | year=1991 | pages=159n, 212n, 213n, 298n}} and {{cite journal | url=https://ndupress.ndu.edu/Portals/68/Documents/jfq/jfq-78/jfq-78_111-124_Clodfelter.pdf | title=The Limits of Airpower or the Limits of Strategy: The Air Wars in Vietnam and Their Legacies | first=Mark | last=Clodfelter | journal=Joint Force Quarterly | volume=78 | number= | date=July 2015 | pages=111&ndash;124}}</ref>

== Later years and honors ==
<!-- not sure what this means, 'A' is for publications? ignore Littauer was named a member of the Am. Phys. Soc. A in 1980<ref name="DeG-bio"/> he was a member of the APS all along per <ref name="sps-chair-bio"/>  -->[[List of fellows of the American Physical Society (1972–1997)|In 1991]], Littauer was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="aps-fellow-1991"/> The citation for the achievement read, "For outstanding contributions to accelerator control systems, architecture and electronics, and in the use of feedback to cure instabilities."<ref name="aps-fellow-1991">{{cite web | url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=L&year=2023&unit_id=&institution= | title=APS Fellow Archive: L | publisher=American Physical Society | access-date=February 21, 2024 }}</ref>

In 1995, Littauer was awarded the [[Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators]].<ref name="cerncourier-1995"/> The citation on the prize, also from the American Physical Society, read, "For his many contributions to accelerator technology, in particular his innovative conception and implementation of a mechanism to provide multifold increases in the luminosity of single-ring colliding beam facilities by the establishment of separated orbits of opposing, manу-bunch, particle beams. [...] the concept has been adopted, equally successfully, at the other high energy physics facilities of the world."<ref name="aps-award-1995">{{cite web | url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Littauer&first_nm=Raphael&year=1995 | title=1995 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators Recipient | publisher=American Physical Society | access-date=March 27, 2023}} <!-- earlier announcement at https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/199505/honors.cfm --></ref>

Littauer became a professor emeritus of Physics,<ref name="cc-clicking"/> but remained active in efforts to improve undergraduate education at Cornell.<ref name="cornell-obit"/> As part of this he maintained an interest in networked classroom technology.<ref name="abrahamson"/><ref name="cc-clicking"/>

Littauer died on October 19, 2009, at his home in  [[Trumansburg, New York]].<ref name="ij-obit-2009">{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-ithaca-journal-obituary-for-raphael/138567303/ | title=Obituaries/Local: Raphael Littauer | newspaper=The Ithaca Journal | date=October 21, 2009 | page=4A | via=Newspapers.com}} Also available [https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/theithacajournal/name/raphael-littauer-obituary?id=28500294 here].</ref>  His wife Alexandra had died four years earlier.<ref name="alexandra-obit">{{cite news | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/theithacajournal/name/alexandra-littauer-obituary?id=50226337 | title=Obituary: Alexandra Littauer | newspaper=The Ithaca Journal | date= March 17, 2005}}</ref>

== Selected publications ==
* ''Accelerators: Machines of Nuclear Physics'' (Anchor Books, 1960) [co-author with Robert R. Wilson]
* ''Pulse Electronics'' (McGraw-Hill, 1965)
* ''[https://archive.org/details/airwarinindochin0000corn/page/n15/mode/2up?view=theater The Air War in Indochina]'' (Beacon Press, 1972) [co-editor with Norman Uphoff]
